title: Shabari
hook: the old tribal woman who tasted the berries first

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama breaks. The steady hero asks the trees where Sita went, and the poem doesn't hide it. Even he wept.

A grandmother knows you're coming. She's been cooking since morning, and before she serves you anything she tastes every pot, a little spoon from each, because she will not hand you something that isn't right. Now put her deep in a forest, very old, living alone in a small hermitage. Her teacher died years ago. Before he died, he told her: stay here. One day Rama will come. So she stayed. Every morning, for years, she swept the path and gathered fruit, just in case today was the day. And one day two dusty princes walk up the path, one of them still grieving.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER TASTES EVERY POT.` → `ONE DAY RAMA WILL COME.` → `SHE SWEEPS THE PATH FOR YEARS.`

segments.voice: Her name is Shabari. The name marks her as a woman of the Shabara people, a forest community: not a princess, not a priest. In Valmiki's Ramayana she's a devoted ascetic, a disciple of the sage Matanga. She welcomes Rama and Lakshmana, washes their feet, and offers them fruits and roots she has gathered from the forest. Then, having seen the one she waited for, she gives up her body and rises to the heaven where her teachers went. That's the oldest version: short, respectful, luminous. Then the story kept growing, the way stories do when people love them. In later devotional tellings, sung across India for centuries, Shabari gathers wild berries for Rama and bites each one first, so she can keep the sour ones back and give him only the sweet. In most of Indian life, you wouldn't offer anyone food you'd already bitten, let alone a king, let alone God. And Rama eats them gladly. Lakshmana, in some tellings, hesitates. Rama doesn't. Hindu devotion, bhakti, keeps coming back to this scene because it says the gift is measured by the love in it, not the rules around it. An old forest woman, outside every hierarchy, feeds God half-eaten berries, and it's one of the most treasured meals in the whole story. In the Ramcharitmanas, the sixteenth-century Hindi retelling by Tulsidas, Rama even sits with her and teaches her the nine kinds of devotion. The palace had feasts. The forest had this.
screen: `SHABARI: A FOREST WOMAN WHO WAITED.` · `VALMIKI: SHE OFFERS FRUITS AND ROOTS.` · `LATER: SHE TASTES EACH BERRY FIRST.` · `THE GIFT IS MEASURED BY THE LOVE.`

segments.voice: Remember the last time someone fed you with love: not a restaurant, a person, like a parent's lunchbox, a friend's terrible first attempt at a recipe, a neighbor's plate at the door. Taste it again, and notice how little it mattered that it wasn't perfect. Then picture one person you could feed simply, a cup of tea, a piece of fruit, and see yourself handing it over the way Shabari does: humble, and choosing the sweet ones.
Shabari. The old woman of the forest who waited years for Rama, and fed him the best she had.
Your line: the sweet ones. Only the sweet ones went to Rama. That's day fifty-four.

howItsDone: Shabari's story is sung in devotional songs and retold in Ramlila plays and temple talks as an image of simple, humble devotion; in Gujarat, a site near Subir in the Dangs is venerated by many as the place where she met Rama.
